C0.quote: select one member of the group based on nominations from within
C0.note: Selection of a group member by aggregating nominations; impartial selection mechanisms.

C1.quote: a deterministic mechanism with an additive performance guarantee
C1.note: Main results are additive guarantees (upper and lower bounds) for impartial mechanisms. The lower bounds come from an axiomatic impossibility result. Impartiality is an incentive (strategyproofness-type) property, so it is SB. There are no complexity or running-time results, so AL does not apply.

C2.1.quote: takes such a nomination graph as input

C2.2.quote: the more general approval setting, where outdegrees can be arbitrary
C2.2.note: Input is a directed graph in which each vertex's out-neighbourhood is its nomination (approval) set. The paper itself calls this the approval setting, and plurality is the special case of outdegree one.

C2.3.quote: motivated not to reveal their true opinion on who should win

C2.4.quote: motivated not to reveal their true opinion on who should win
C2.4.note: Text says submitted nominations may differ from true opinions. The formal model has no separate notation for held attitudes.

C3.1.quote: the outgoing edges of a vertex have no influence on its selection
C3.1.note: The impartiality analyses consider a voter changing its outgoing edges, i.e. possible misreports. The additive-guarantee analyses evaluate the submitted graph as given.

C3.2.note: The intro motivates impartiality as allowing voters to express true opinions. It never states that voters submit them.

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare, satisfaction, cost or distortion for voters is used.

C5.1.quote: the indegree of the choice of f differs from the maximum indegree
C5.1.note: Outcomes are evaluated by additive approximation of the maximum indegree. This is not framed as welfare, satisfaction, efficiency, representation or distortion.

VOT.quote_behav: motivated not to reveal their true opinion on who should win
VOT.note: Voters' possible profitable deviations motivate and define impartiality, which is strategic. In the additive-guarantee analyses, nominations are taken as exogenous inputs. Voters' knowledge of others is never specified.

CAN.note: Candidates coincide with voters; no separate candidate actions.

DES.note: Mechanisms are designed by the authors; no designer choice or objective is modelled within the model.

C8.1.quote: a change of the outgoing edges of some vertex v does not change
C8.1.note: Impartiality is a strategyproofness-type property: a vertex's own selection is independent of its own nominations.

C9.1.note: Real-world settings (papal conclave, FIFA awards) appear only as motivation. The abstract and introduction state formal results only, and there is no conclusion section.

C1.reason: Impartiality is a strategyproofness-type property studied as a property (SB), while the paper has no algorithmic or complexity results that would warrant AL.

C2.2.reason: The paper explicitly frames the nomination input as the approval setting, so APPR fits better than OTH.

C3.1.reason: The impartiality proofs explicitly consider a voter deviating in its nominations, while the guarantee analyses take the input as given.

C6.VOT.reason: Voters are treated as potential deviators in the impartiality analyses but as given inputs in the guarantee analyses, so MIXED fits better than either NS or STRAT.

C8.1.reason: Since voters are coded MIXED, C8 applies, and impartiality is a strategyproofness-type concept (DOM).

C8.2.reason: The paper names the property impartiality but never calls it strategyproofness or dominant strategies.

C9.1.reason: The quotes B lists are motivation or restatements of formal tightness results, not claims about institutions, voter well-being, or which rule to use.

C9.2.reason: C9.1 is N, so C9.2 is NA.
